extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York (citizens and delegates considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for the structure, composition, and powers of a federal Senate (qualifications, appointment method, equality of representation, size/term, and functions) intended to justify the proposed U.S. constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: National representation reduces partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A national representation, being an emanation from a greater variety of interests and in much more various proportions than are to be found in any single State, will be much less apt to espouse either of them with a decided partiality than the representation of any single State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Because national representatives aggregate a wider range of interests, they are less likely to favor any single local interest (e.g., landed or mercantile). Use this principle to assess whether representation will be broadly representative rather than capture-prone by narrow local factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation limited to times, places, and manner; qualifications fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of the national government would be expressly restricted to the regulation of the TIMES, the PLACES, the MANNER of elections. The qualifications of the persons who may choose or be chosen ... are defined and fixed in the Constitution, and are unalterable by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes procedural election power (time/place/manner) from substantive franchise/eligibility qualifications. When evaluating federal electoral powers, ensure they do not purport to alter constitutional qualifications of electors or candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confining places of election would disenfranchise and fail to secure an elite preference
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of securing to the rich the preference apprehended, but by prescribing qualifications of property either for those who may elect or be elected. ... The policy of confining the places of election to particular districts would be as subversive of its own aim as it would be exceptionable on every other account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test/example: limiting polling locations would tend to disenfranchise remote electors rather than concentrate power in the wealthy; the only effective way to entrench an elite would be property qualifications, which are not within the proposed power. Use geographic-accessibility effects to judge proposals about polling location rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in time of elections is a public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives ... may be found by experience to be of great importance to the public welfare, both as a security against the perpetuation of the same spirit in the body, and as a cure for the diseases of faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages listed: enables total dissolution/renewal at once, reduces contagion of example, supports regular rotation in the Senate, and facilitates convening the legislature at a stated period. Evaluate staggered vs. uniform election timing against these goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senatorial qualifications: older age and longer citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualifications proposed for senators ... consist in a more advanced age and a longer period of citizenship. A senator must be thirty years of age at least ... and the former must have been a citizen nine years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: greater extent of information and stability of character; reduces risk of foreign influence from recent immigrants. Use age and citizenship-period thresholds as levers to increase presumed experience and attachment to national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment by State legislatures favors select appointment and state agency
rubrics_metrics.description: That which has been proposed by the convention [appointment by State legislatures] is probably the most congenial with the public opinion. It is recommended by the double advantage of favoring a select appointment, and of giving to the State governments such an agency in the formation of the federal government as must secure the authority of the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing appointment mechanisms, weigh trade-offs between 'select' appointment (insulation, deliberation) and democratic direct election; consider the institutional link this creates between state and federal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of state representation in the Senate as compromise and protector of state sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The equality of representation in the Senate ... being evidently the result of compromise between the opposite pretensions of the large and the small States ... is at once a constitutional recognition of the portion of sovereignty remaining in the individual States, and an instrument for preserving that residuary sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View equal state votes as both political compromise and mechanism to prevent consolidation of states into a single centralized republic. Evaluate equal representation by its capacity to protect smaller units and retard overcentralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a double security: concurrence of two bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate, as a second branch of the legislative assembly, distinct from, and dividing the power with, a first, must be in all cases a salutary check on the government. It doubles the security to the people, by requiring the concurrence of two distinct bodies in schemes of usurpation or perfidy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design criterion: bicameral concurrence raises the difficulty of usurpation/corruption. Use presence and competence of a second chamber to evaluate protections against concentrated power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate should be less numerous and longer-tenured to resist passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A body which is to correct [the propensity of assemblies to yield to sudden passions] ought itself to be free from it, and consequently ought to be less numerous. It ought, moreover, to possess great firmness, and consequently ought to hold its authority by a tenure of considerable duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: set senate size smaller and terms longer to promote deliberation and stability; compare alternative sizes/terms by their impact on susceptibility to factional or transient pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate supplies legislative knowledge and corrects blunders
rubrics_metrics.description: Another defect to be supplied by a senate lies in a want of due acquaintance with the objects and principles of legislation. ... A well-constituted senate provides ... an increase of security for fidelity to the object of government and knowledge of the means by which that object can be best attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion focuses on expertise, continuity, and institutional memory: evaluate whether the chamber's composition and incentives promote study of law, continuity of policy, and reduction of ad hoc/repealing legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate mitigates harmful mutability and provides continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutability in the public councils arising from a rapid succession of new members ... points out, in the strongest manner, the necessity of some stable institution in the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences of mutability outlined: loss of foreign respect, internal incoherence of law, advantage to speculators. Use this to judge whether proposed term lengths/turnover rates will produce stable policy conducive to investment and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate preserves national character and sensibility to foreign opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a select and stable member of the government, the esteem of foreign powers will not only be forfeited by an unenlightened and variable policy ... but the national councils will not possess that sensibility to the opinion of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a chamber's composition and permanence will foster a consistent, respectable foreign policy and attention to international opinion that can check transient domestic impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer-tenured body needed so responsibility can cover long-term measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility, in order to be reasonable, must be limited to objects within the power of the responsible party, and in order to be effectual, must relate to operations of that power, of which a ready and proper judgment can be formed by the constituents. ... An assembly elected for so short a term as to be unable to provide more than one or two links in a chain of measures ... ought not to be answerable for the final result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication: for policy objectives requiring multi-year chains of measures, accountability is best assigned to a body with sufficient permanency to plan and be judged on long-term results. Use term length to align responsibility with feasible scope of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as safeguard against popular temporary errors and delusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an institution may be sometimes necessary as a defense to the people against their own temporary errors and delusions. ... In these critical moments, how salutary will be the interference of some temperate and respectable body of citizens, in order to check the misguided career ... until reason, justice, and truth can regain their authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally, the senate acts as a brake on transient popular passions that might lead to self-harm. Assess whether institutional features (insulation, deliberation, slower turnover) will reliably perform this moderating role without becoming permanently anti-democratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent: long-lived republics had a senate
rubrics_metrics.description: History informs us of no long-lived republic which had not a senate. Sparta, Rome, and Carthage are, in fact, the only states to whom that character can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical analogies cautiously: the presence of long-standing senatorial institutions in surviving republics is offered as supportive evidence for creating a stable council; weigh differences in context but treat the precedent as a relevant datum in institutional design.
